unitTargets: ▸  I can describe a vector by its magnitude and direction, and resolve it into components.
▸  I can add vectors, at right angles and at any angle, and report the resultant with a direction.
▸  I can split a projectile’s motion into two axes that share one time.
▸  I can solve flat, angled and different-height launches using one shared time.
keyTerms: ▸  North of East, East of North
howItWorks: The left column names what to record. The open space beside it is for the board: write, sketch, label. Use as much of it as the slide needs.
Worked examples print the problem. Copy the setup and every step from the board, and carry units the whole way.
Your Turn: work it in the box first, then check against the board before the next slide.
Every vector answer carries a direction. Every number carries a unit.
Projectile problems: +y is up, so down is negative. Neglect air resistance.

sectionsContent.title: Vectors & Vector Basics (Review)
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe a vector by its magnitude and direction, name a direction two ways, and resolve a vector into x- and y-components.

problem.label: VECTOR · MAGNITUDE · DIRECTION
key: Vector: magnitude AND direction; drawn as an arrow.
Magnitude: the size or length; never negative, zero is possible.
Direction: which way it points, given relative to a reference direction.
A number alone does not specify a nonzero vector.

cues: Length as magnitude, angle as direction

problem.label: DRAWING A VECTOR
key: Choose a scale first. Tail = start, tip = end.
Arrow length = magnitude. Angle measured from a reference axis at the tail.
Tip points the way the vector acts.
Sketch: arrow with tail, tip and angle theta from the axis labeled.

problem.label: RESOLVING A VECTOR INTO COMPONENTS
key: Ax = A cos theta   (adjacent to theta)        Ay = A sin theta   (opposite theta)
theta measured from +x. Components let you add vectors.
Sketch: right triangle with A as the hypotenuse, Ax along x, Ay along y.

problem.label: EXAMPLE — RESOLVING A DISPLACEMENT
problem.statement: A hiker walks 50 m at 30° above the horizontal. Find the x- and y-components.
key: Given: A = 50 m, theta = 30°.   Find: Ax and Ay.
Check: Ax² + Ay² = A², allowing for rounding.

problem.label: DEGREES AND COMPASS DIRECTIONS
key: From an axis: measure from the horizontal or vertical reference.
Compass bearing: “40° North of East” starts at east, then turns toward north.
One vector, two names: 40° N of E = 50° E of N, because 40° + 50° = 90°.

cues: The relationship between the two angles

problem.label: EXAMPLE — CONVERTING THE ANGLE
problem.statement: A vector points 40° North of East. Express its direction as an angle East of North.
key: East of North = 90° − North of East
Answer: 50° East of North (same direction as 40° North of East).

cues: Work it first, then check the board

problem.label: YOUR TURN — A HIKING BEARING
problem.statement: A hiker walks at 65° East of North. Express this as an angle North of East.
key: North of East = 90° − East of North
Answer: 25° North of East.

cues: Work it first, then check the board

problem.label: QUICK CHECK — CONVERT AND RESOLVE
problem.statement: A force of 20 N acts at 70° East of North. Find its angle North of East, then resolve its components.
key: theta = 90° − 70° = 20° North of East

sectionsContent.summaryPrompt: In your own words: why is a number alone not enough to describe a vector, and what do you need to resolve one into components?
selfCheck: I can draw a vector and label its tail, tip and angle.
I can convert North of East to East of North.
I can resolve a vector into x- and y-components.
sectionsContent.summaryKey: Sample: a number alone gives only a size, so a vector also needs a direction. To resolve one you need its magnitude and its angle from a reference axis, then Ax = A cos theta and Ay = A sin theta.

sectionsContent.title: Vector Addition
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can add two vectors, at 90° or at any angle, and state the resultant’s magnitude and direction.

problem.label: ADDING PERPENDICULAR VECTORS
key: Tip-to-tail; the resultant joins the original tail to the final tip.
Magnitude: R = √(A² + B²)        Direction: theta = arctan(B/A), from the A direction.
Only for perpendicular vectors.

cues: Common error — a magnitude with no direction

problem.label: EXAMPLE — PLANE IN A CROSSWIND
problem.statement: A plane flies 80 km/h east relative to the air. A wind blows 20 km/h north. Find the plane’s velocity relative to the ground.
key: theta = arctan(20/80) = 14°
Answer: 82.5 km/h at 14° N of E.  Always report magnitude AND direction.

problem.label: ADDING VECTORS AT ANY ANGLE
key: 1 • Resolve: Ax = A cos theta, Ay = A sin theta
2 • Add: Rx = sum of the x-components, Ry = sum of the y-components
3 • Recombine: R = √(Rx² + Ry²), theta = arctan(Ry/Rx)
Use the signs of the components to choose the correct quadrant.

cues: Add x to x and y to y
Extra digits kept until the final answer

problem.label: EXAMPLE — TWO FORCES ON A BOX
problem.statement: A 40 N force acts east, and a 30 N force acts 60° above east. Find the resultant force.
key: R = 60.8 N at 25.3° N of E

cues: Work it first, then check the board

problem.label: YOUR TURN — TWO DISPLACEMENTS
problem.statement: Walk 30 m east, then 40 m at 45° above east. Find the resultant displacement.
key: Answer: R ≈ 64.8 m at 25.9° N of E.

cues: Work it first, then check the board

problem.label: PRACTICE — THREE FORCES ON A CRATE
problem.statement: Three ropes pull on a crate: 30 N east, 40 N north, and 20 N at 30° south of west. Find the resultant force.
key: Answer: R ≈ 32.6 N at 67.1° N of E.   (Added problem: not on the slides.)

sectionsContent.summaryPrompt: In your own words: when can you use the right-triangle shortcut, and what do you do when you cannot?
selfCheck: I can add two perpendicular vectors.
I can add vectors at any angle using components.
I can state a resultant with magnitude and direction.
sectionsContent.summaryKey: Sample: use R = √(A² + B²) when the vectors are perpendicular. Otherwise resolve each vector, add the x-components and the y-components, then recombine.

sectionsContent.title: Projectile Motion (All Types)
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can split a projectile’s motion into two axes, solve the vertical motion for time, and use that time horizontally.

problem.label: PROJECTILE · TRAJECTORY · RANGE
key: Projectile: an object moving under gravity alone after release.
Trajectory: the path it follows; a parabola when horizontal velocity is nonzero.
Range: horizontal distance from launch to landing.
Model: no air resistance, constant g = 9.8 m/s². Horizontal and vertical motion are independent and share the same time.

cues: Horizontal velocity with no air resistance
Common error — a force is needed to keep it moving sideways

problem.label: NO HORIZONTAL FORCE NEEDED
key: Gravity acts downward. With no air resistance, vx stays constant.
Inertia: no horizontal net force means no horizontal acceleration.
Common error: a force is needed to keep it moving sideways. It is not.

problem.label: THE FLAT LAUNCH
key: Horizontal: vx = vix = constant;  x = vix t
Vertical drop: viy = 0;  h = ½gt²   (h = positive drop distance)
Time to land: t = √(2h/g).   Equal time steps → equal horizontal spacing.

cues: Vertical motion first, for the shared time

problem.label: EXAMPLE — ROLLING OFF A TABLE
problem.statement: A ball rolls off a 0.80 m table at 2.5 m/s. How long until it lands, and how far does it travel horizontally?
key: Given: h = 0.80 m;  vix = 2.5 m/s, viy = 0.
Horizontal: x = vix t = 2.5(0.404) = 1.01 m
Answer: t ≈ 0.40 s,  x ≈ 1.0 m

cues: Work it first, then check the board

problem.label: YOUR TURN — OFF A HIGHER SHELF
problem.statement: A marble rolls off a 1.25 m shelf at 3.0 m/s. How far from the shelf does it land?
key: Answer: x ≈ 1.5 m from the shelf.

cues: Time of flight, and when it applies

problem.label: LAUNCHING AT AN ANGLE
key: Components: vix = vi cos theta;  viy = vi sin theta
Time of flight: t = 2viy/g   (same launch and landing height only)
Range: R = vix t
At the peak: vy = 0, vx unchanged.

cues: Time depends on viy, range on both components

problem.label: EXAMPLE — A KICKED SOCCER BALL
problem.statement: A ball is kicked at 18 m/s at 30° above level ground. Find its time of flight and range.

cues: Resolve first, then the level-ground formulas
Work it first, then check the board

problem.label: YOUR TURN — A LAUNCHED ARROW
problem.statement: An arrow is shot at 45 m/s at 40° above level ground. Find its range, neglecting air resistance.

problem.label: WHEN LAUNCH AND LANDING DIFFER
key: Not symmetric about the peak; the level-ground shortcut fails.
Choose +y upward. Landing lower means more time descending than ascending.
At the peak: vy = 0;  t_apex = viy/g.        Height gained: Δy = viy²/(2g).
Total flight time: solve 0 = y₀ + viy t − ½gt² when the landing surface is y = 0.

cues: Height above launch, then above ground

problem.label: EXAMPLE — MAX HEIGHT FROM A CLIFF
problem.statement: A rock is launched at 20 m/s at 35° from a 15 m cliff. Find its maximum height above the launch point.
key: viy = 20 sin 35° = 11.47 m/s;  vy = 0 at the top.
Δy = viy²/(2g) = 11.47²/(2·9.8) = 6.71 m above the launch point
(Above the ground: 15 + 6.71 = 21.7 m.)

cues: The quadratic and the root to keep

problem.label: EXAMPLE — LANDING BELOW THE LAUNCH
problem.statement: The same rock (20 m/s, 35°, from a 15 m cliff) lands on the ground below. Find its total time of flight.
key: y(t) = y₀ + viy t − ½gt²   →   0 = 15 + 11.47t − 4.9t²
Keep the positive root: t ≈ 3.28 s ≈ 3.3 s. The negative root is before release.

cues: The quantity shared by both axes

problem.label: THREE STAGES, ONE IDEA
key: 1 • Horizontal launch: viy = 0; find time from the drop.
2 • Angled, level ground: resolve vi first; t = 2viy/g.
3 • Different heights: find the peak or solve the full vertical-position equation.
Every projectile problem: resolve, solve vertically, then use the same time horizontally.

sectionsContent.summaryPrompt: In your own words: explain how one projectile moves with constant velocity in one direction and accelerates in the other, and what the two motions share.
selfCheck: I can find the time from the vertical motion and use it horizontally.
I can solve a flat, an angled and a different-height launch.
I can find the peak height and the total flight time from a cliff.
sectionsContent.summaryKey: Sample: horizontally the velocity is constant (no horizontal force); vertically it accelerates at g. The two motions share the same time, found from the vertical motion.
